 Florida Dengue Cases Jump by 100 to 624 as Hillsborough's Weekly Count Nearly Triples After a Brief Slowdown
 Published Nov 17, 2026 8:34 PM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 RHONA WISE | AFP via Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Florida added 100 locally acquired dengue cases in the week of Nov. 1 to 7, bringing the state's 2026 total to 624, according to the Florida Department of Health's Week 44 arbovirus report . Hillsborough, Pinellas and Pasco counties accounted for 92 of the new cases.
 Hillsborough County reported 61 new cases, nearly triple the 22 it logged the week before. Pinellas County added 29, its highest weekly count this year, WUSF reported .
 For families in Tampa, Brandon, Clearwater and St. Petersburg, the new numbers change the practical message from last week. A brief slowdown had raised hopes that cooler weather was winding the outbreak down, but the virus is still circulating, and backyard mosquito control still matters.
 Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving Florida's 2026 dengue outbreak. Information may change as state and county health officials release additional findings. Case data are through Nov. 7, 2026, from the Florida Department of Health's Week 44 report, released Nov. 13. Hillsborough County announced the extension of its local state of emergency on Nov. 13. 
 A Rebound After the Slowest Week Since August
 MedicalDaily previously reported that Hillsborough's dengue cases had risen at their slowest pace since August , with 22 new infections in the week ending Oct. 31 and 524 cases statewide. That week now looks like a pause rather than a turning point.
 Hillsborough's total stands at 468 cases since the outbreak began in July, including the September death of an 80-year-old Tampa woman. The county recorded 62 cases in all of October, so the latest week nearly matched that monthly total.
 Pinellas has now reported 109 cases, about half of them in October alone, and Pasco has six. Orange and Miami-Dade each added four, bringing them to 14 and 16. Florida has also logged 422 travel-associated cases this year , most linked to travel from Cuba.
 Reporting Lag Clouds the Picture
 The jump may not mean transmission sped up in early November. The state notes there is often a delay between when symptoms begin and when a case is reported. The Department of Health said, "The number of new locally acquired dengue cases under investigation has decreased in recent weeks." It added that "as investigations are completed, updates will be reflected in the weekly case counts." 
 That suggests some of the 100 cases may be infections that began earlier and were confirmed recently. By onset date, the state lists 294 local cases with symptoms starting in September and 137 in October. October's count will likely grow as late reports arrive.
 Officials have not said how many of the new cases had symptoms in November. Without that breakdown, it is not possible to tell whether the outbreak is accelerating or the count is catching up on earlier infections. Fewer investigations also do not mean the outbreak itself is shrinking.
 The official count is also likely an undercount, since many people infected with dengue never feel sick and are never tested.
 Brevard and Central Florida Stay on Watch
 Brevard County remains under a mosquito-borne illness advisory, the state's lower warning level, which the Florida Department of Health in Brevard announced in mid-October after confirming a locally acquired case, WFTV reported . The state still lists one local case in Brevard, and the advisory was highlighted again in WFIT's local news report , which warned that recent heavy rain may increase the mosquito population.
 Statewide, 12 counties are under advisories, and nine are under the higher-level alert.
 Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise extended the county's local state of emergency through Nov. 19, according to a county release . Mosquito surveillance shows dengue virus in mosquitoes in many neighborhoods , the county said, and crews are increasing treatments by air and ground.
 The county is shifting tactics as the season changes. Wide-area spraying by small planes was expected to wrap up last week, while helicopter spraying and targeted ground treatments continue in neighborhoods with cases, Bay News 9 reported . Hillsborough is coordinating with Lee and Manatee counties and plans to continue mosquito control efforts through at least March.
 "We really do wanna make sure that we stop this completely, really stamp it out," said Josh Bellotti, Hillsborough County's director of engineering and operations. The goal is to keep dengue from becoming endemic, or present year after year.
 Protecting the Household as Holidays Approach
 The Aedes aegypti mosquito that spreads dengue bites mainly during the day and breeds in small amounts of standing water near homes. Households can empty flowerpot saucers, buckets, toys, tires, and pet bowls at least weekly, especially after heavy rain, and keep window and door screens repaired.
 Families hosting outdoor Thanksgiving gatherings can use EPA-registered repellent. Hillsborough residents can report problems to Mosquito Management Services at (813) 635-5400 and sign up for alerts about where aerial treatments are happening.
 Dengue often starts with high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, rash and muscle or joint pain. People with symptoms should see a clinician and mention where they live or traveled. The CDC advises avoiding aspirin and ibuprofen if dengue is suspected, since they can raise bleeding risk.
 Warning signs can appear as the fever breaks. Severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, or extreme tiredness need emergency care. Older adults, infants, pregnant people and anyone who has had dengue before face a higher risk of severe illness. Uninsured residents can contact their county health department about testing and care.
 The state's next weekly report is expected this week. MedicalDaily will report whether the Tampa Bay rebound continues and whether Hillsborough extends its emergency again after Nov. 19.
 Developing Story Timeline
 Nov. 13, 2026: The state's Week 44 report shows 100 new local cases and 624 statewide. Hillsborough extends its emergency through Nov. 19.
 Oct. 25 to 31, 2026: Week 43 data show 22 new cases in Hillsborough, its fewest since August, and 524 statewide.
 Oct. 16, 2026: Brevard confirms a locally acquired case, and the Florida Department of Health in Brevard issues a mosquito-borne illness advisory.

 Key Questions Answered
 How many local dengue cases does Florida have? 624 locally acquired cases in 2026, through Nov. 7, according to the Florida Department of Health.
 How many were added in the latest week? 100, including 61 in Hillsborough, 29 in Pinellas, and two in Pasco.
 Is the outbreak speeding up? It is unclear. The state says reporting delays mean some new cases may have started earlier, and fewer cases are under investigation.
 Is there a new advisory in Brevard County? No. Brevard's advisory dates to mid-October after one local case, and it remains in effect.
 Which counties are under a mosquito-borne illness alert? Alachua, Citrus, Duval, Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Pasco, Pinellas, and Seminole.
 What are dengue warning signs? Severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme tiredness. Seek emergency care.
 How can households reduce risk? Empty standing water weekly, use EPA-registered repellent, and keep window and door screens repaired.
